_meta.purpose: Every claim about a named competitor tool or AI detector published on metegpt.com links to a dated primary source recorded here; article citations like (EV-winston-ai-detector-01) resolve to the matching id below.
_meta.screening_note: Only sources screened INCLUDED under the protocol appear here. Excluded categories -- off-topic, affiliate roundups with no disclosed methodology, sources unverifiable on the collection run, duplicates, and vendor-seeded 'astroturf' review content -- are withheld by design; the protocol never cites them. Each page's collection_sweep publishes the exclusion COUNTS (including how many sources were screened out as astroturf) so the screening is auditable without republishing any withheld source or naming any third party.
_meta.field_note: Internal working fields (coder identities, curator annotations, flow IDs) are omitted. The citable record for each item is its claim, verbatim quote, source URL and source date.
_meta.cross_listed_note: A source that supports claims on more than one page appears under each; unique_sources counts distinct ids, page_appearances counts listings.

entries.claim: An independent 16-tool humanizer test (4 detectors: Originality AI Turbo, Winston AI, ZeroGPT, Sapling) found StealthGPT and WriteHuman were the only two tools that reduced AI-detector scores while keeping output readable; several other named tools (Phrasly AI, Surfer SEO, Smodin AI) scored 100% AI probability on the same test. entries.claim: Originality.ai's own dated test of Duey.ai (single 800-1000 word ChatGPT sample, four detectors) recorded a wide spread of results per detector and warned the rewritten output became incoherent even where detector scores dropped — an example of the detector-score-vs-readability tradeoff. This test predates the Turnitin Aug-2025 update by one week.

entries.platform: Originality.ai company blog (third-party test of a different vendor's tool, stated methodology)

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed 14-tool study (Weber-Wulff et al., 2023, International Journal for Educational Integrity) found that no AI-text detection tool it tested reached 80% accuracy, only five of the fourteen surpassed 70%, and the tools showed a systematic bias toward classifying output as human-written rather than AI-generated.
entries.quote: the available detection tools are neither accurate nor reliable... a main bias towards classifying the output as human-written rather than detecting AI-generated text
entries.source_date: 2023-07-10 (v2; journal publication International Journal for Educational Integrity, Vol. 19, Article 26, 2023)
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (International Journal for Educational Integrity / Springer; also on arXiv, Weber-Wulff et al., 8 authors including Debora Weber-Wulff, HTW Berlin)

entries.claim: The same peer-reviewed 14-tool study found that content-obfuscation techniques (paraphrasing/editing AI text) significantly worsen detector performance across the tools tested — direct academic support for the 'paraphrased/humanized text lowers reliability' disclosure this page must make about detectors generally, including pattern-based ones.
entries.quote: Content obfuscation techniques significantly worsen the performance of tools
entries.platform: peer-reviewed journal (International Journal for Educational Integrity / Springer; Weber-Wulff et al. 2023)

entries.claim: A 2025 NBER/Becker Friedman Institute working paper (Jabarian & Imas) comparing four AI-text detectors on 1,992 human and 1,992 AI-generated passages across six genres found the three commercial tools (Pangram, GPTZero, Originality.ai) held false-positive rates under 1% on medium/long text, but the open-source RoBERTa baseline misclassified human text at a 30-78% false-positive rate depending on scenario — concrete cross-detector evidence that detector method/vendor materially changes real-world reliability, not just marketing claims.
entries.quote: false positive rates of approximately 30-78% across scenarios [for RoBERTa]... All three commercial tools maintained false positive rates below 1 percent [on medium/long passages]
entries.platform: university research institute publication (Becker Friedman Institute, University of Chicago; underlying NBER Working Paper No. 34223, authors Brian Jabarian and Alex Imas)

entries.claim: The same NBER/BFI study found accuracy for all three commercial detectors (Pangram, GPTZero, Originality.ai) degrades on short passages, with texts under roughly 50 words the hardest case for every tool tested — direct academic corroboration of the 'short text is a structurally noisy signal for any detector' disclosure this page must make.
entries.quote: Accuracy varied significantly by text length, with short passages (under 50 words) proving most challenging
entries.platform: university business-school research review (Chicago Booth Review, summarizing Jabarian & Imas / NBER Working Paper No. 34223)

entries.claim: The same study found GPTZero and Originality.ai occupy a 'secondary tier' relative to Pangram, with a real tradeoff between them: minimizing false positives favors GPTZero, while maximizing detection of AI-written text favors Originality.ai — concrete evidence that different named detectors optimize for different error types, which is the academic basis for recommending a cross-check with a second, differently-tuned detector rather than trusting one tool's verdict.
entries.quote: OriginalityAI and GPTZero constitute a secondary tier among commercial detectors with partial strengths, making the choice between the two dependent on the user's priority: minimizing false positive rate favors GPTZero, while maximizing ability to distinguish AI from human text favors OriginalityAI.
entries.platform: university research institute publication (Becker Friedman Institute, University of Chicago; NBER Working Paper No. 34223)

entries.claim: Pangram Labs' own dated, methodology-disclosed test of 30 AI-detection tools (9 AI-generated texts from ChatGPT-4o/Gemini 2.0/Claude 3.7, 3 human-written control texts, pass thresholds of >=75% AI-score for AI text and <=25% for human text) found GPTZero correctly identified 7 of 9 AI texts (78%) and Originality.ai 7 of 9 (77%), versus the vendor's own tool (Pangram) and Copyleaks each scoring 9 of 9 — registered as a vendor's own competitive test, not adopted as a neutral ranking, since Pangram is also a detector vendor being compared favorably to its rivals.
entries.quote: Pangram Labs: 9/9 AI texts (100%), 3/3 human texts (100%)... GPTZero: 7/9 AI texts (78%), 3/3 human texts (100%)... Originality.ai: 7/9 AI texts (77%), 3/3 human texts (100%)
entries.platform: vendor company blog (Pangram Labs; author Max Spero, Pangram co-founder — disclosed as a competing detector vendor's own test of its rivals, methodology stated)

entries.claim: NPR education reporting (Dec 2025) documents named students now routinely running their own homework through multiple AI-detection tools before submitting it, specifically because of fear of false accusation — direct journalism evidence for the 'cross-check with more than one detector' behavior this page recommends, independent of any single detector vendor's self-interest.
entries.quote: She now runs all her homework assignments through multiple AI detection tools before she turns them in.
entries.platform: NPR (national news journalism)

entries.claim: CalMatters journalism (2025) documents named community-college and CSU students describing the emotional and practical impact of AI/plagiarism-detector false flags, plus a named instructor noting Turnitin is not good at catching the strongest actual tipoff of AI use (fabricated quotes/hallucinations) — corroborates that detector verdicts are an imperfect proxy signal, not a certainty verdict, from the educator side as well as the student side.

entries.platform: CalMatters (nonprofit newsroom journalism; quoting Adam Kaiserman, College of the Canyons English instructor, and separately Nilka Desiree Abbas, a San Bernardino Valley College student who described being falsely accused)

entries.claim: A named, dated false-positive incident (Rolling Stone, June 2023): a UC Davis student was flagged by Turnitin's AI detector on a genuine, human-written assignment, and the same reporting quotes Turnitin's own marketing claim of 98% accuracy alongside its own acknowledged 'small risk of false positives' -- a concrete, journalism-verified case pairing a vendor's self-stated accuracy figure with a real misfire.

collection_sweep.note: Documents the discovery sweep for this page's most recent collection run. 'Included this run' counts newly surfaced sources only; a page's published entries can also include earlier verified sources re-checked in this run.

entries.claim: Winston AI's own homepage markets a 99.98% accuracy figure with no disclosed test-set size, human-to-AI sample ratio, or operating threshold -- only a one-line dataset claim.
entries.quote: “99.98% accuracy rate” ... “The most trusted AI detector” ... “Trained on the largest dataset of human reviewed data to minimise false positives.”
entries.platform: Vendor primary source (gowinston.ai homepage) -- self-interested, Winston's own marketing claim

entries.claim: Winston AI's own help-center page names three factors it says reduce real-world accuracy below its claimed rate (short text, non-prose document types, human/AI-humanizer editing) and explicitly warns against treating a score as a guilty verdict.
entries.quote: “99.98% accuracy rate based on benchmark testing across models like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, and LLaMA” ... “no detector should be treated as an automatic guilty verdict.”
entries.platform: Vendor primary source (Winston AI Help Center) -- self-interested

entries.claim: Winston AI's own scoring-explainer page states that its published percentage is a confidence level in authorship, not a measurement of what share of a text is AI-written -- a distinction its marketing rarely surfaces.
entries.quote: “a score of 80% human and 20% AI doesn't mean that only 20% of the content was generated by AI; rather, it means that Winston has a 80% confidence level that the content was created by a human.”
entries.platform: Vendor primary source (gowinston.ai) -- self-interested

entries.claim: Winston AI's Terms & Conditions (Limitations of Liability, Section 23) explicitly disclaim any guarantee of accuracy and state a score of 90 can still be wrong roughly 1 in 10 times -- directly in tension with the 99.98% marketing claim.
entries.quote: “The accuracy of the returned result is not guaranteed.” ... “A score of 90, for instance, indicates that our detection tool may mistakenly label content as AI-generated approximately 1 time out of every 10.”
entries.platform: Vendor primary source (gowinston.ai/terms-conditions) -- self-interested by definition (Winston's own legal contract)

entries.claim: Winston AI's current pricing runs a credit-metered model across three paid tiers plus a 14-day/2,000-credit free trial, with detection and plagiarism-checking consuming credits at different per-word rates.
entries.quote: Essential -- $10/mo billed annually or $18/mo monthly, 80,000 credits/mo; Advanced -- $16/mo annually or $29/mo monthly, 200,000 credits/mo; Elite -- $26/mo annually or $49/mo monthly, 500,000 credits/mo. AI detection: 1 credit/word; plagiarism check: 2 credits/word.
entries.source_date: undated (live pricing page, current as fetched)
entries.platform: Vendor primary source (gowinston.ai/pricing) -- self-interested

entries.claim: Winston AI sells its own content-authenticity certification product, HUMN-1, which audits only a small random monthly sample of a site's pages (10 or 30, tier-dependent) rather than every published page.
entries.quote: “The first human content certification for websites and blogs” ... “Audit of 10 random posts on your website every month” (HUMN-1 tier) ... “Audit of 30 random posts on your website every month” (HUMN-1+ tier).
entries.source_date: undated (live product page, current as fetched)
entries.platform: Vendor primary source (gowinston.ai) -- self-interested

entries.claim: Winston AI, an AI-content detector vendor, publishes its own blog content reviewing AI humanizers and states plainly that most humanizers will not beat premium detectors including its own -- a detector company marketing against the tools built to beat it.
entries.quote: “most AI Humanizers will not bypass premium AI detectors, so it is really important to do your due diligence before buying a subscription.” ... Humanize AI Pro “Doesn't bypass premium AI detectors like Winston AI and Turnitin.”
entries.platform: Vendor primary source (gowinston.ai) -- self-interested (a detector vendor rating competitor humanizer products, direct commercial interest in the verdict)

entries.claim: Winston AI's own 2023 blog post on false positives explains detection is probabilistic and cautions educators against treating a score as proof of wrongdoing, but does not acknowledge the elevated false-positive risk for non-native English writers documented in the wider academic literature (EV-winston-ai-detector-15).
entries.quote: “the assessments are based on probabilities” ... “Educators using AI detectors must use caution when taking an assessment as absolute evidence of any wrongdoing.”
entries.platform: Vendor primary source (gowinston.ai) -- self-interested

entries.claim: A peer-reviewed-venue study (Frontiers in Education, University of Wisconsin-Madison Dept. of Bacteriology) measured Winston AI directly and found an F1 of 0.83 on human-vs-AI classification but a 45.8% false-positive rate on genuinely human text, concluding it is 'unusable to monitor students' as a standalone tool.
entries.quote: Human vs. AI: “Accuracy: 0.80, Precision: 0.74, Recall: 0.93, F1: 0.83.” Winston “failed badly when examining human text, flagging nearly half as false positives” (45.8% false-positive rate), making it “unusable to monitor students” standalone.
entries.platform: Academic (Frontiers in Education journal article, authors Timothy Paustian and Betty Slinger, UW-Madison)

entries.claim: A competitor (GPTZero) review reports that when it ran a 22,000-word human-written novel with two AI-generated paragraphs inserted on the opening page through Winston AI, Winston returned a 100% human-written verdict for the whole document, missing the inserted AI content entirely.
entries.quote: “it still categorized the entire text (which included the new, AI-generated paragraphs on the opening page) as 100% human-written.”
entries.platform: Competitor-authored review (GPTZero, a rival detector vendor) -- self-interested

entries.claim: A competitor (Originality.ai) ran three 100%-ChatGPT-5-generated samples through Winston AI and reports Winston correctly flagged only one of the three as fully AI (100% AI), while scoring the other two at 87% AI and just 3% AI respectively.
entries.quote: Blog post: “100% AI & 0% Human-written.” Promotional email: “87% AI & 13% Human-written.” E-Book extract: “3% AI & 97% Human-written.” All three samples were ChatGPT-5-generated; Winston's own detector called only one “100% Likely AI.”
entries.platform: Competitor-authored review (Originality.ai, a rival detector vendor) -- self-interested

entries.claim: An independent test with disclosed methodology (own dataset of ChatGPT-written, human-written, and human-edited-ChatGPT articles, no humanizers/paraphrasers used) measured Winston AI at 83.33% accuracy and an F1 of 85.71%, with false positives concentrated in complex/technical-topic articles.
entries.quote: “Accuracy: 83.33%, Precision: 75%, Recall: 100% (no false negatives), F1-Score: 85.71%.” “No AI humanisers or paraphrasers were used and the edited articles weren't put through an AI detector.” False positives “mostly identified in articles that had a slightly more complex and technical topic.”
entries.platform: Independent blog test (captainwords.com) -- disclosed methodology but exact sample size/word counts not stated

entries.claim: DetectArena, a crowdsourced blind-pairwise-comparison benchmark platform, lists Winston AI with a 0.5% false-positive rate and an Elo rating of 1551 as of this run, alongside Winston's own 99.98% claimed-accuracy figure for comparison.
entries.quote: “Claimed Accuracy: 99.98%” ... “Elo Rating: 1551” ... “False Positive Rate: 0.5%.” “DetectArena ranks AI detectors using blind pairwise voting. Users compare two tools on the same text without knowing which is which, then vote on which performed better.”
entries.source_date: undated (live leaderboard page, current as fetched)
entries.platform: Independent third-party benchmark platform (detectarena.ai) -- crowdsourced, disclosed blind-voting methodology, but per-tool vote count/sample size is not shown on this page

entries.claim: SupWriter, a competing AI-writing/detection-bypass vendor, ran a disclosed 150-sample test (six AI models, five content categories) and reports that of 40 verified human-written samples, Winston AI flagged 4 as AI-generated -- a 10% false-positive rate on that defined sample.
entries.quote: “We tested Winston AI with 150 samples across six AI models and five content categories.” “Out of 40 verified human-written samples: 4 flagged as AI-generated (10% false positive rate).”
entries.platform: Competitor-authored test (SupWriter, which sells its own AI humanizer and a dedicated 'bypass-winston-ai' product) -- self-interested

entries.claim: The landmark Stanford-led detector-bias study (Liang et al. 2023, Patterns/Cell Press) found AI detectors as a class flagged 61.3% of authentic non-native-English (TOEFL) essays as AI-generated versus near-zero for native-English essays -- general detector-class evidence, since the seven commercial detectors tested were not individually named (Winston AI's inclusion is unconfirmed).
entries.quote: “While the detectors accurately classified the US student essays, they incorrectly labeled more than half of the TOEFL essays as 'AI-generated' (average false-positive rate: 61.3%).”
entries.platform: Academic (Patterns / Cell Press, Liang, Yuksekgonul, Mao, Wu, Zou, Stanford)
